title: Guru ka Bagh, 1922
hook: volunteers took police beatings without striking back, and the world saw it

segments.voice: Yesterday, the keys, and your line was first battle won. Did you keep one peaceful resolve? Today ends a week that began with a long memory in London and has turned toward the gurdwaras. Day nine hundred eighty-seven.

Dry branches, an axe, and a kitchen fire that needs feeding. In a village outside Amritsar there is a gurdwara called Guru ka Bagh, the Guru's garden, with land around it where acacia trees grow. Sikh volunteers go out to cut wood for the langar, the free kitchen. The custodian who holds the shrine says the land and the trees are his. The police arrest the woodcutters for theft. And then more volunteers keep coming, walking toward the police lines with their hands at their sides.
screen: `WOOD FOR THE LANGAR FIRE.` → `ARRESTED FOR THEFT.` → `MORE VOLUNTEERS KEEP COMING.`

segments.voice: First, the quarrel. Like Nankana and Tarn Taran earlier this week, Guru ka Bagh was in the hands of a mahant, a hereditary custodian, and the reformers said a Guru's shrine belonged to the whole panth. The wood was a small thing. Who owned the garden was not. Second, the jathas. Groups of volunteers set out each day from the Akal Takht in Amritsar, having taken a vow to stay peaceful. At the garden the police met them with heavy sticks and beat them to the ground. Accounts written at the time describe men falling, getting up, and being struck again, without raising a hand. Third, the witness. Charles Freer Andrews, an English clergyman, went to see for himself. He wrote that he watched the blows fall on men who did not strike back, and that the sight brought the crucifixion to his mind. His account was printed and read far beyond Punjab. That is how the world came to see it. Fourth, the root. In the Asa di Var, at Ang 470 of the Guru Granth Sahib, Guru Nanak says that sweetness and humility are the essence of every virtue and all goodness. The volunteers walked to the garden humbly, with no weapon and no curse. But humble did not mean bowed. They walked into the blows on purpose, and when they were knocked down, they got up. That's today's line: beaten, unbowed. And that finishes a week that ran from Udham Singh and Bhagat Singh to the SGPC, Tarn Taran, Nankana and the keys.
screen: `WHO OWNED THE GARDEN?` · `JATHAS VOWED TO STAY PEACEFUL.` · `AN ENGLISH CLERGYMAN WATCHED.` · `SWEETNESS AND HUMILITY.` · then, large: `BEATEN, UNBOWED.`

segments.voice: Two minutes as a witness. Sit, and let your breath slow. C. F. Andrews didn't march. He went, he watched, and he wrote down what he saw. Bring to mind one time you saw someone stand firm while they were treated unfairly: at school, at work, on a street, in the news. Picture it plainly, without adding anything. Breathe in, and remember what they did. Breathe out, and ask: if I told this to one other person, what would I say? If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. The bell holds the time.
Bagh, garden: the Guru's garden near Amritsar, where volunteers walked into police beatings without striking back, and the account of it traveled the world. Today's word.
Your line: beaten, unbowed. Today, refuse to hit back once: if someone pushes you with words, stand where you are and answer without a blow of your own. Day nine hundred eighty-seven.

howItsDone: Sikhs remember Guru ka Bagh as one of the peaceful campaigns of the gurdwara reform movement; the gurdwara near Amritsar keeps its memory, and the story is told in histories of the Akali movement.

notes: Editor: replaced the Ang 1378 Farid 'do not strike back' salok, which day 985 had just used, with Ang 470 (sweetness and humility); cut 'centuries earlier' and the garbled 'part of the hook that says' line; new witness practice and reworded carry, because the jaw-and-shoulders, let-it-pass practice and carry repeated days 984–985; removed the stale note about day 986 missing.

Week end: the teach closes by naming the week's days 981–986 from the index (Udham Singh, Bhagat Singh, the SGPC, Tarn Taran, Nankana, the keys). The hook's 'Nankana and Tarn Taran earlier this week' assumes those days' scripts tell those stories.
